records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
ASCOTTISH council has signed a secrecy agreement with an AI data centre developer, a Freedom of Information request has revealed. West Lothian Council signed the secretive non-disclosure agreement (NDA) with an unknown firm in the 2025-26 financial year.
While the majority of local authorities said they had not signed any NDAs, three councils which have live planning applications for hyperscale data centres would not confirm or deny if they had done so.
These were Dumfries and Galloway, where potentially the world’s largest data centre is proposed at Chapelcross; North Ayrshire, where a data centre is proposed at Hunterston; and East Lothian, where data centres are planned near Dunbar and at the former Cockenzie power station.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Herald letters
THE SNP policy of installing 18GW (gigawatts) of wind power in Scotland to meet a maximum demand of only 4GW means a massive constraint payment debt under periods of high winds. This explains why electricity bills in Scotland are double those on the continent. Too much power for the current demand means high levies being paid to power companies.
However, what is surprising is the deafening silence from opposition politicians at Holyrood.
They are not demanding to know why, under dunkelflaute conditions, wind farm operators are not required to provide free electricity to Scottish energy users when a lack of wind means renewable generators fail to do what’s claimed on the tin, forcing the use of expensive gas turbines to keep the lights on in Scotland.
Why does the SNP always favour big business at the expense of the Scottish consumer?
Ian Moir, Castle Douglas.

records.bodyText:
Strathy South wind farm project is located to the south of SSE Renewables' operational Strathy North wind farm, approximately 12km to the south of Strathy village.
In November 2021, planning permission was granted consent by Scottish Ministers to construct and operate 35 turbines, known as Strathy South Wind Farm, (with a ground to blade tip maximum height of 200m metres), in lands near Strathy, Sutherland.
In December 2024, the final decision to proceed to construction in spring 2025 with commercial operations expected in late 2027.
SSE Renewables made the final investment decision to proceed with construction of the 208MW Strathy South wind farm after more than a decade of development.
Once complete, with 35 Vestas V162-6.2 wind turbines, Strathy South will be capable of powering around 200,000 homes annually.
Part of the development was to establish a community investment fund as part of the Strathy South project, which is valued at £1m per year for the lifetime of the wind farm.
In addition, Strathy South will have a vast biodiversity net gain (BNG) through the restoration of peatland at the site and the removal of over 1000 hectares of non-native commercial forestry.
At 38.1% projected wind load factor is expect from the installed capacity of 208MW
Strathy South Compulsory Purchase Order
The Scottish Ministers have confirmed SSE Renewables’ Compulsory Purchase Order (“CPO”) to secure necessary land for the transport of turbine components to Strathy South wind farm.
A complete set of the submitted CPO documents is available below, including the Statement of Reasons, which provides additional detail on the rationale for the use of these powers. The documents relating to the Inquiry are available on the Scottish Government’s Planning and Environmental Appeals Vision website at the following link Scottish Government - DPEA - Case Details (scotland.gov.uk)— in Strathy.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Cumberhead Wind Farm is an operating 50 MW onshore wind energy facility located within Cumberhead Forest in South Lanarkshire.
The site features 12 Nordex N133/4800 wind turbines (consisting of ten 83-metre and two 110-metre hub height units).
Construction began following planning and forestry approvals (managed alongside land partner Bidwells), and the farm entered commercial operation in March 2023.
It is owned by Octopus Renewables Infrastructure Trust and supplies clean power through a novel corporate power-purchase arrangement—notably launching with ties to companies like Kimberly-Clark to help decarbonize energy intensive manufacturing.
The electricity feeds into the transmission grid via the Cumberhead Collector Substation (completed by SP Energy Networks in late 2022), tying into nearby lines toward the Coalburn Grid Substation.
Cumberhead West Wind Farm: A neighboring expansion and development project (partnered by 3R Energy and ScottishPower Renewables) sits adjacent to the original site. It is designed to add 21 larger turbines (up to 200m tip height) with a 126 MW capacity and a 40 MW energy storage facility.— in Douglas, South Lanarkshire.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Just outside Thornton, near Glenrothes, there was once an ambitious mining project that was expected to transform the future of Fife.
Rothes Colliery was planned as one of the National Coal Board's great new superpits.
Work began in 1946, and expectations were enormous. The mine was designed to produce an incredible 5,000 tons of coal every day and was expected to operate for around 100 years.
So confident were the planners that the new town of Glenrothes was developed partly to provide homes for the thousands of workers expected to be employed there.
On 30 June 1958, Queen Elizabeth II officially opened the colliery.
Its two enormous concrete winding towers became familiar landmarks across the Fife landscape.
But beneath the ground, things were going badly wrong. The mine encountered serious geological difficulties, thinning coal seams and persistent flooding. Water continually entered the workings, making it increasingly difficult and expensive to extract coal.
Despite the enormous investment and optimism, Rothes Colliery closed in May 1962, just five years after production began.
The two towering concrete structures remained standing for another three decades, overlooking the landscape and reminding po people of an extraordinary industrial ambition.
In March 1993, they were finally demolished.
Today, only remnants of the surface infrastructure remain.
Imagine building an entire new town around the promise of a mine that was expected to last a century, only for it to close after five years.
Rothes Colliery: a forgotten chapter in Fife's industrial history.
Text & Photos by Brian Mackie.— at Thorton.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Most people when thinking about the mine shafts at Leadhills think about the Glengonner Mine, Susannah Mine and other areas around the perimeter of the village but there were shafts right in the middle of the village.
One of these was next to the Curfew Bell at the junction of Store Brae and Ramsay Road.
Cockburns Shaft was used latterly to pump water from the Meadowfoot Vein. A water pressure pump was installed in 1833 to pump from 70 fathoms (420ft. 120mtrs) but it was not a new shaft then but fitted into an earlier shaft shown on older maps.
The old photo of the Curfew Bell has a fenced off area where the shaft is.
This was one of the shafts checked in 1991 when work was done on a lot of the shafts within the village (and Wanlockhead) arranged by Scottish Enterprise, Clydesdale Council and Nithsdale Council as they were then.
The photo and report are from the published result of the survey and shows any work carried out if required at the sites.
There were over 40 sites within and around Leadhills alone checked and made safe at that time.
Text & Photos by Ken Ledger— in Leadhills.

records.bodyText:
An interesting fun fact.
The West Calder site is planned to have a 250MW BESS (Battery Energy Storage System).
The main strategy for these is to charge up during the off-peak times with the objective that they discharge during peak times. As far as I understand it "off-Peak", with many suppliers, are the hours between 23:30 and 5:50 - the rest of the day is at the full rate. 
Currently, for domestic suppliers the off-peak rate is about one fifth of the full rate - this is because demand dips overnight to the extend that the main supplier has to compensate the wind farms etc. for disabling their wind turbines to protect the grid from excess supply. I assume a similar reduction will be available for business customers.
Now, under normal operating procedure, the aim is to run batteries  between 20 and 80% capacity (in order to maintain battery health and prolong life); that means only 60% of the 250MW is the forecasted usable amount (150MW).
However, assuming this amount was only to cover the peak times, the site would need additional power during off-peak whilst the batteries were recharging. There's a huge over simplification here but assuming that 150MW covers 18 hours (Peak); extending to 24 hours means the consumption will likely be 200MW.
Given that the average household consumption is around 30KW this means that 200MW is enough for around 6,667 private dwellings.
And I read somewhere they're looking at potentially 20 Hyper Data Centres in Scotland?
Scotland's current electrical generating capacity stands at 18.1GW. if all the proposed hyper data centres had the demand then they would need approximately 4GW or 22% or our entire generating capacity.
Given that we're all being encouraged to switch to Electric Vehicles and Air-Source Heat pumps that's going to potentially increase domestic demand by up by maybe 40% by 2030. 
How is this even possible?
